item.title: Bit Flip
item.description:
What you just did

Computers store every number as a row of on/off switches called bits. Each switch is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on up to 128. Eight of them together make a byte, which can hold any whole number from 0 to 255. The row of 0s and 1s under the number is that byte, written the way a computer stores it. So when you made 37, you wrote 00100101, which is 37 in binary.

item.title: Campus Route
item.description:
How a map app finds the fastest route

The shortest-looking route is often not the fastest one, which is why map apps don’t just pick the path with the fewest turns. They use a method worked out by the computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra in 1956 and published in 1959.

It works like this: start where you are, at 0 minutes. Then, again and again, take the closest place whose time isn’t final yet, mark its time as final, and see whether going through it gives any of its neighbors a faster time. When the destination’s time becomes final, it is guaranteed to be the fastest possible. Press Watch a computer solve it after a puzzle to see each step on the map.

item.title: Code Word
item.description:
How the clues work

Every guess must be a real word with the same number of letters as the answer. After each guess, every letter gets a mark: a filled dot means the letter is in the right spot, a ring means the word has that letter somewhere else, and a dash means it doesn’t (or not that many times). The letter buttons keep track of what you have learned.

About the words

Each day’s word is a computing term that comes up in everyday life, from the cloud to cookies to chatbots. When the puzzle ends, you’ll see a short, plain explanation of what it means.
